item.title: Microservices best practices every automation engineer should know
item.description: Discover microservices best practices to build resilient systems. Learn what the best patterns look like and how workflow automation fits into the process.
item.dc:creator: n8n team
item.content:encoded:
A microservices architecture breaks an application into small, independent services that each handle a specific function and communicate through APIs. If one service fails, the others ideally keep running instead of taking down the entire application. It makes systems more failure-resistant, but only if those microservices are designed to fail safely.

Microservices best practices help you control how your services depend on and communicate with each other, so a failed API or unavailable database doesn’t trigger a chain reaction.

Define clear service boundaries

When designing microservices, decide where one service stops and another begins. A useful rule of thumb is to draw those boundaries around a distinct business capability.

Domain-driven design is a practical approach to draw boundaries. It groups related business logic into a bounded context, or a defined part of the business with its own rules, language, and data. The single responsibility principle is also useful — each service should own one business capability rather than sharing that responsibility with others.

For example, an order service might take care of order creation and each order’s status, while a payment service handles charging and refunds. Keeping those responsibilities separate also makes each service independently deployable, so changing your payment logic doesn’t require you to release unrelated parts of the application.

If different services share the same responsibility, even a small change might force you to update APIs, move data, and coordinate deployments across all of them.

💡
In n8n, sub-workflows can help you separate service-specific orchestration into smaller, reusable workflows. Each sub-workflow owns its own service-calling logic and error handling, making failures easier to isolate and troubleshoot.

Build resilience into service-to-service calls

As your services start depending on one another, service-to-service communication becomes part of your potential failure surface. A service can be healthy and still fail to complete its task because another one times out, rejects a request, or becomes temporarily unavailable. 

With synchronous communication, one service waits for another to respond, so a slow dependency can delay the caller even when the caller itself is working normally. If you don’t need an immediate response, asynchronous communication can reduce that dependency. For example, one service can place work on a message queue for another process when it’s ready.

Designing for these failures is a core part of distributed system resilience, where the wider system can keep doing its job even when one dependency has a problem. That’s why you use microservices architecture patterns like circuit breakers, retries, and bulkheads. Each addresses a different failure mode.

Circuit breaker pattern

A circuit breaker watches for repeated failures and temporarily stops sending requests once they cross a threshold. It doesn’t repeatedly wait for a service that’s unlikely to respond, but instead it lets the caller fail fast for a period and gives the dependency time to recover.

💡
n8n’s error workflows give you workflow-level failure handling instead of a stateful circuit breaker. You can configure an error workflow separately in Workflow Settings — if the main execution fails, n8n runs that workflow starting with the Error Trigger. You can use it to log the failure or start recovery logic.

Retry with exponential backoff

Some failures are only temporary, so if a service times out for a few seconds, trying again may be enough to complete the request. Retries make sense for transient faults, like timeouts or rate limits. However, retrying immediately can put pressure on a struggling service.

Exponential backoff handles this by increasing the delay after each failed attempt. 

💡
For more straightforward retries, n8n’s Retry On Fail setting lets you set the maximum number of tries and a fixed waiting period between them. If you want the delay itself to increase after every failure, you can build that logic into the workflow with a loop and the Wait node.

Bulkhead pattern

A bulkhead pattern isolates one failing part of your system and prevents it from consuming resources that other tasks depend on. For example, if Service A becomes unresponsive, requests to Services B and C can still use their own resources.

Route traffic through an API gateway

As your service count grows, letting clients call each microservice directly can create coordination issues and become difficult to manage. Every client has to know which endpoint handles its corresponding request, and changes to a service can force changes in the clients depending on it.

For example, imagine a checkout app that has to know all the separate URLs for:

  • Orders
  • Inventory
  • Payment
  • Shipping services

If one of those services moves or changes its API, you may also have to update every client that calls it. 

An API gateway pattern solves this by giving clients one entry point. The gateway receives a request, decides which services should handle it, and forwards it to the right place. It keeps the internal structure of your system behind a stable interface, so you can change or reorganize services without exposing every change to the client.

The gateway needs to be constantly available and resilient itself. If every request passes through one gateway, that instance can become a new single point of failure. You can tackle this by using multiple instances or regions and using load balancing to direct traffic through another gateway if one becomes unavailable.

Make failures observable across the system

Finding the failure source becomes challenging in a microservices architecture because one request can cross multiple independently running services before you notice the final error. For example, if a checkout request moves through inventory, payment, and fulfillment, a failure at the end doesn’t immediately tell you which service caused it or what happened to the data along the way.

In monolithic architecture, where most application logic runs inside one larger app, you can often trace the problem from one set of logs. With microservices, you can use distributed tracing to follow the same request across services and centralized logging to bring their separate logs into one searchable data store.

n8n is an AI-native, source-available workflow automation platform that can orchestrate calls across APIs and services in visual workflows, with code available when you need custom logic.

Orchestrate service calls with full execution visibility

Inspect every run, follow the path of each execution, and debug failed calls node by node with n8n

Sign up for free

n8n allows you to improve visibility across your project’s microservices. For example, after receiving a Redis event, n8n checks whether the services work within acceptable error rates. If so, two related microservices are called sequentially and the Redis key is removed. If one of the microservices fails, an Error Key is incremented: If there are too many errors within a pre-defined TTL, the workflow stops with an error.

It offers visibility across parts of the process it orchestrates. In the Executions view, you can inspect previous workflow runs, follow the path an execution took, and check the inputs and outputs at each node to see where data changed or a call failed. You can also load data from a previous execution back into the editor to debug and rerun it.

💡
n8n can also work along with the distributed microservices. If you use message queue brokers like RabbitMQ, Redis, Kafka and others, n8n can read and send messages through the same channel as the other parts of your app.

Make resilience part of the architecture with n8n

Resilience is most effective when you design for failure proactively. That means deciding how your services communicate, where failures should stop, and how you’ll identify and understand what happens when a request doesn’t complete as expected.

n8n can complement that architecture by giving you a visible orchestration layer around your service calls. Your microservices still own their business logic and infrastructural resilience, while n8n coordinates the workflow between them through HTTP calls, branching, retries, and failure handling where appropriate.

As those dependencies grow, it might be helpful to explore n8n’s guide to event-driven microservices.

item.title: Batch processing patterns for workflow automation at scale
item.description: Learn batch processing patterns for scalable workflows, including chunking, rate limits, retries. Discover the tools that put these patterns into practice.
item.dc:creator: Yulia Dmitrievna
item.content:encoded:
Batch processing gets complicated with large loads. A workflow that breezes through 200 records might stop on 20,000. You’ll suddenly find yourself faced with memory limits, API quotas, and the question of what actually finished.

The patterns in this guide will help you keep those problems from derailing the whole workflow.

Batch processing in workflow orchestration

Batch jobs often start life as scripts, with job scheduling handled separately for each one. That works well enough at first, but add a few systems and soon you’re juggling separate schedules, credentials, logs, and failure handling. When something breaks, figuring out where (and what already ran) can become a job of its own.

With workflow orchestration, those jobs can run across apps, databases, and APIs from one place. The workflow defines when a batch runs, how data moves between systems, and what happens when a step fails. That gives you a single execution path to monitor and troubleshoot instead of a collection of scripts running independently.

Batch processing vs. stream processing

The biggest difference between batch and stream processing is timing. Batch processing collects data and processes it in groups, while stream processing handles data continuously as it arrives. They both have uses:

  • When to use batch processing: When results don’t need to be immediate, like with scheduled data syncs, reports, or bulk updates
  • When to use stream processing: When timing is essential and you can accommodate the always-on infrastructure and added operational complexity that come with faster speeds

Three batch processing patterns

Once volume goes up, a single batch may put more pressure on memory, APIs, and downstream systems than they can comfortably handle. These batch processing patterns give you more control over how much work happens at once, how quickly it moves, and what happens when individual records fail.

Chunking: Splitting large datasets

Chunking breaks a large dataset into smaller groups that move through the workflow one at a time. Instead of asking a downstream system to handle thousands of records in a single batch operation, you might send 100 or 500 at a time.

Smaller batches use less memory and make failures easier to isolate, while larger batches can reduce the overhead of processing each group. The goal is to find a size that keeps the workflow moving without overwhelming the next step.

Rate limiting: Pacing batches within API limits

Smaller batches can still cause trouble if you send them too quickly. Many APIs cap the number of requests they'll accept within a given period, so a fast workflow could start receiving rate-limit errors even when each individual request is valid.

You can handle rate limits by adding pauses between requests or batches and configuring retries when an API asks you to slow down. 

💡
In n8n, you can handle rate limits; the Loop Over Items and Wait nodes can control the pace. You can also avoid rate limiting with the HTTP Request node’s built-in Batching option.

Per-item error handling and retry

One bad record shouldn't set a healthy batch back. Per-item error handling lets the workflow separate failed items from successful ones, then retry or route those failures without repeating work that's already complete. 

Deduplication can add another safeguard when a rerun might contain records you’ve already processed. It’s one part of idempotency: designing a workflow so retrying the same work doesn’t create unintended duplicate results. 

💡
n8n gives you several ways to handle execution errors, including node-level error behavior and dedicated error workflows. For batch jobs, that means you can preserve successful work, capture enough context to investigate failures, and decide whether an item should be retried, skipped, or handled separately.

Scaling batch processing with n8n

The best batch size and processing speed depends on the workload, available memory, API limits, and number of running executions. 

n8n is an AI-native, source-available automation platform that can help teams scale batch processing. It’s been tested with up to 220 workflow executions per second on a single c5a.large instance running a two-node workflow.

Scale batch processing without stitching together separate tools

Split, aggregate, loop, wait, and deduplicate on one canvas with n8n

Sign up for free

Instead of assembling separate batch processing tools, you can handle most of the steps directly in the workflow:

  • Split Out node: Turns a list inside a single item into individual items that can move through the workflow separately
  • Aggregate node: Combines separate items or selected fields back into a single list when the next step needs them together
  • Loop Over Items (Split in Batches) node: Sends a set number of items through the workflow at a time, giving you direct control over batch size
  • HTTP Request node: Sends batched data to APIs and gives you control over request behavior when there’s no dedicated integration
  • Wait node: Pauses execution between batches or requests, helping you stay within API rate limits
  • Remove Duplicates node: Filters repeated items before they move to the next step
  • Debug executions: Loads previous execution data to debug failed runs (available on n8n Cloud and registered Community plans)

You can also split workflows into sub-workflows to manage memory limits. These sub-workflows return a restricted amount of data to the parent workflow.

For larger self-hosted workloads, queue mode lets you distribute workflow executions across workers. That gives you another lever for scaling throughput as volume grows, without changing the batching logic inside the workflow.

Build batch processing workflows that can handle the load

As batch workloads grow, the problems usually show up at the edges: too many records hitting one step, an API that can’t keep pace, a failure that leaves you wondering what needs to run again. 

Chunking, rate limiting, and per-item error handling give you ways to control each of those pressure points. n8n brings those controls into the workflow itself, letting you adjust how data moves without rebuilding the process around it. 

Start with a batch size your systems can comfortably handle, watch how the workflow behaves under load, and tune from there.

FAQ

How do you make batch processing safe to rerun?

A failed batch shouldn't force you to choose between starting over and risking duplicate work. The key is making each operation idempotent. That way, processing the same record twice produces the same result instead of creating a duplicate.

One approach is using upserts when writing to a database or data warehouse. Instead of blindly inserting each record, the workflow updates an existing record when its unique identifier already exists. Checkpointing can help too: Save a checkpoint as batches finish (for example, mark processed records as “done”) so a failed job can resume from the last known successful point rather than replaying the entire dataset.

How do you choose the right batch size?

Start with the limits around the workflow. Consider the memory and computing resources available to the workflow, the request limits of downstream APIs, and the amount of data each item contains.

Then test under a realistic load. If batches consume too much memory or trigger API errors, reduce their size or processing rate. If the workflow spends more time managing tiny batches than processing data, increase the batch size. Tune the size further as the workload changes.

Where is batch processing commonly used?

Batch processing works well for jobs where some delay is acceptable and there’s enough data to make processing records together worthwhile. Common examples include scheduled ETL, data transformation, database migrations, bulk API updates, and loading records into a data warehouse.

For applications like fraud detection, where new events may need an immediate response, real-time data or stream processing is usually a better fit.

item.title: Build Safer n8n Agents and Workflows with Google Gemini 4 Carbon
item.description: Gemini 4 Carbon is out and it's now available in n8n. Google is calling it its strongest model yet, with big gains in coding, long-running agentic work and cybersecurity. In Google's results, it posts a 53.9% on AutomationBench, a benchmark for automation work, topping
item.dc:creator: Liam Hampton
item.content:encoded:
Gemini 4 Carbon is out and it's now available in n8n. Google is calling it its strongest model yet, with big gains in coding, long-running agentic work and cybersecurity. In Google's results, it posts a 53.9% on AutomationBench, a benchmark for automation work, topping the results which makes it a good fit for n8n. If you're building AI agents in n8n, this is one to try.

Checkout the benchmarks Google published.

Benchmarks reported by Google. Source: Gemini 4 Carbon announcement.

What Carbon brings to your n8n agents

Google's announcement focuses on three areas, and each one maps neatly onto how you build in n8n.

Strong on security. Security is top of mind for this launch. Carbon leads its benchmarks across the defence lifecycle: finding vulnerabilities (88.2% on SEC-bench Pro), checking which ones are exploitable (54.8% on ExploitGym) and patching them (71.0% on CWE-bench). If your team runs security workflows in n8n, this one's for you.

Built for the long haul. Carbon handles long, multi-step tasks. Google reports that internal team runs have lasted for days on complex engineering problems, pushing through dead ends instead of stopping like previously seen. In n8n, that means your agents can work through more steps and tool calls before losing the thread.

More reliable agents. Agents in n8n often read inputs that you don't or cannot control, such as inbound emails, web-hook payloads, form submissions and scraped pages. Any of these can carry hidden instructions that can be used to hijack your agent. On Gray Swan's prompt injection benchmark, Carbon resisted every attack (0.0% success rate, down from 0.7% for Argon). Although this is a real improvement, no model is completely resistant to malicious attacks at scale, so keep your security protocols in place.

Example use case

A security alert lands via web-hook. Your agent reads it, pulls the related logs, checks it against known issues, sets a priority, and posts a summary to Slack for your on-call engineer. The alert text is untrusted input, which is exactly where prompt injection resistance pays off.

The web-hook hands the alert to an AI Agent running on Gemini 4 Carbon, which uses two tools before posting its summary to Slack.

How you can use Gemini 4 Carbon in n8n

Open an AI Agent node, add the Google Gemini Chat Model, and pick Gemini 4 Carbon from the model list. It's also available in the standalone Google Gemini node. Plug in the tools your agent is allowed to use, add memory if it needs context, and you're good to go.

On n8n Cloud, you can use Carbon through Gateway credits, so there's no separate provider account or extra billing. On self-hosted, just add your own Gemini API key.

Already using Gemini 4 Argon? You don't need to switch everything over. Use Carbon for the agent steps that need heavy reasoning, and keep Argon or a lighter model for simple jobs like classifying or formatting.

What it costs

Google has launched Carbon at the same introductory price as Argon: $2 per million input tokens and $10 per million output tokens, rising to $4 and $20 once the introductory period ends (November 30, 2026). Full details are in Google's announcement.

Overall, Gemini 4 Carbon gives your n8n agents more staying power on long tasks and better protection against the messy, untrusted input they deal with every day. Build your first workflow and get started with Google Gemini 4 Carbon today.

Happy building!

item.title: Meet Nod: a standalone personal agent from n8n Labs that runs on your computer
item.description: Nod gets stuff done for you. It works in your apps and on any website, asks before it acts, and uses the AI provider you choose.
item.dc:creator: Ophir Prusak
item.content:encoded:
Today we're releasing Nod as a research preview from n8n Labs, a new team within n8n that experiments with ideas outside our core product. Nod is a standalone app, separate from n8n, that runs on your computer. It's a personal agent with its own computer and browser: you tell it what you need, and it works in your apps and on websites until the job is finished. It's open source, and it uses the AI provider you choose.

You can download Nod for Mac and Windows. The code is on GitHub under an open-source licence.

Why we built it

n8n has always been about helping people automate work. That was true before AI and it's true now. AI lets software take on more kinds of work, but the goal is the same.

A lot of what people build in n8n is multiplayer: processes that a team or a business shares and runs on a shared n8n instance. Nod is for a single player. It's built for one person, connects to that person's accounts, and gets their jobs done, whether the job is for their business or their household.

Nod also lives outside n8n. It's a separate app from n8n and from the agents you can build inside n8n, and you don't need an n8n account to use it. You install it on your computer, connect your accounts and ask for something. There's no server or cloud service to set up first.

When we sat down with early testers, many of them placed Nod in the same spot on their own: their chat assistant is where they think and write, n8n runs their shared processes, and Nod takes the ongoing jobs that are theirs alone.

Nod is a n8n Labs experiment, and it doesn't change the direction of n8n. Work on n8n and the n8n agent continues as planned. Building and using Nod has taught us a lot about how AI can take on more of the work people do, and we're releasing it as a research preview so more people can use it and show us where it should go next.

What Nod does

Because Nod has its own computer (a sandbox that runs locally) and browser, it can finish jobs that a chat tool would hand back to you as a to-do list. It works in the apps you connect, such as Gmail, Calendar, Drive and Slack, and on websites that have no integration at all.

Some of the jobs people hand it:

  • Cancel a subscription, turn down the retention offers and ask for your refund
  • Watch a price and tell you when it drops
  • Find a hotel that fits your trip and book it once you say go
  • Sign in to your supplier portals each month, download the invoices, and file them for your accountant
  • Pull last week's numbers from a dashboard that has no way to export the data and put them in your weekly report

Nod also works ahead of you: it reads your connected apps and offers the jobs it could take off your plate. You talk to it in one conversation, in the app or on Telegram or WhatsApp, while it runs several jobs in parallel in the background. Jobs that repeat, like a morning brief or a price check, can run on a schedule.

It gets to know you

Nod remembers months of conversation, so you don't have to keep reminding it what you want. On LongMemEval, a public benchmark for long-term memory, it scored 93.2%, among the best published memory systems.

It learns your preferences as you go, and when you connect Gmail it checks how you write so its drafts sound like you. It also writes down how it got a task done, uses those notes the next time, and fixes them when a site changes. You can see, edit or delete anything Nod keeps about you.

Who it's for

Nod is for anyone who wants to hand the mundane parts of their week to AI: the forms, the follow-ups, the logins and the reminders. Solo operators and freelancers use it for their business, and plenty of people use it for errands at home.

For now you connect your own AI provider, with an API key or your ChatGPT plan, so Nod suits people who are comfortable with that kind of setup. If you use n8n, you can connect your instance so Nod can work with your workflows.

Built to be trustworthy

An agent that can send email and pay with your card has to earn your trust. We designed Nod so you can check how it behaves.

It's yours
Nod is open source under Apache 2.0, and every rule it follows is in the code. It runs on your Mac, your Windows PC or your own server, with the model provider you choose.

It works in its own sandbox
Nod works inside a private virtual machine on your computer, with its own browser. Its data, memory and saved logins stay on the machine running it; your AI provider gets what each task needs.

Only you give it permission
Before Nod sends, pays, posts or deletes anything you didn't ask for, a separate check confirms you asked for it. A web page or an email can't give Nod orders.

The AI never sees your passwords
Your saved logins and cards are encrypted on your machine, and Nod enters them through private forms the model can't read.

Everything is on record
Nod logs every sign-in, card use and action in your apps, along with what each task cost.

The permission check is itself a model and can make mistakes, which is why Nod asks when your words don't cover an action.

What it costs

Nod is open source and free. You pay your model provider for the AI you use, or you can connect an open-source model running on your own computer. Some early testers found tasks cost more than they expected, so cost has been a focus of our recent releases, and the latest one brought it down substantially.

Nod also has guardrails so costs don't run away:

  • Every task shows what it cost, and a finished task ends with a receipt
  • You can set a monthly spending limit
  • Nod checks in with you once a task passes $5, and you can change that amount
  • Each schedule shows its estimated monthly cost

What it doesn't do, yet

  • When Nod is running on your laptop, it stops when the laptop sleeps. Some testers keep it on an always-on Mac mini or run it on their own server, and a hosted version is on our roadmap.
  • Each installation has one owner.
  • It can't make phone calls.

Try it

Download Nod for Mac or Windows, or read the code on GitHub. Then hand it one job from your list. Tell us how it went in the n8n Labs category on the community forum, or with Send feedback in the app.

https://github.com/n8n-io/nod - Github repo
https://nod.n8n.io/docs/ - Nod Docs

item.title: Send contracts for e-signature from n8n, with TurboDocx, Slack approval and SharePoint filing
item.description:
This Verified Node Spotlight is a guest post written by Nicolas Fry, CEO of TurboDocx.

The deal is closed and the contract is ready. It's been sitting in someone's inbox for three days, waiting for an "OK, send it." Once it's finally
item.dc:creator: n8n team
item.content:encoded:
This Verified Node Spotlight is a guest post written by Nicolas Fry, CEO of TurboDocx.

The deal is closed and the contract is ready. It's been sitting in someone's inbox for three days, waiting for an "OK, send it." Once it's finally signed, the PDF ends up in a Downloads folder instead of the shared drive.

n8n can already handle most of that. It can pull the deal data, generate the document, route it for approval, and file it wherever you like. But there hasn't been a native node for the one step that makes a contract a contract: the signature. So the workflow stops there, and someone finishes the job by hand.

In this post, you'll build a workflow that closes that gap. A row in Excel marked Ready to send becomes a generated contract. A manager approves it in Slack. It goes out for signature. When the client signs, the executed PDF is filed in SharePoint and the row updates itself. The signature step runs on the verified TurboDocx node.

What you'll build

The canvas has two parts. One sends contracts, and the other waits for signatures.

Part A: send. This part runs every 15 minutes.

  1. Schedule Trigger starts the run.
  2. Microsoft Excel reads the contract table and keeps only rows marked Ready to send.
  3. Loop Over Items handles one contract at a time.
  4. TurboDocx generates the agreement from your template and converts it to PDF.
  5. Slack posts an Approve & send / Reject message and waits.
  6. If branches on the answer.
  7. TurboDocx sends approved contracts for signature.
  8. Microsoft Excel marks the row Sent or Rejected, and Slack lets the team know.

Part B: file. This part runs when someone signs.

  1. TurboDocx Trigger fires on signature and downloads the executed PDF.
  2. Microsoft SharePoint uploads it to your contracts folder.
  3. Microsoft Excel marks the row Signed, and Slack posts the good news.
👉
Who does what: n8n handles the schedule, the loop, the branching, and moving data between Excel, Slack, and SharePoint. TurboDocx handles the two parts n8n doesn't do natively: turning a Word template into a finished contract, and collecting a legally binding signature.

Before you start

  • An n8n instance. Cloud or self-hosted both work. Start a free trial if you don't have one yet.
  • The TurboDocx node. Install the TurboDocx node directly from the canvas via the Node panel in n8n. You will be prompted to do this if you import the template below.
  • A TurboDocx account. The free tier includes 5 document generations and 5 signatures a month. That's plenty for building and testing.
  • Microsoft 365 with Excel and SharePoint, and credentials for both set up in n8n.
  • A Slack workspace and an approvals channel, such as #contract-approvals.
Try It yourself

Create a free TurboDocx account at TurboDocx.com and start generating documents and sending them for e-signature straight from your n8n workflows. Your account has everything you need to follow this walkthrough end to end. And if you're building quote-to-contract flows, TurboQuote, our CPQ product, brings configure-price-quote into the same document and signature engine.

Import the template to follow along.

Get the workflow

Step 1: Set up your contract queue in Excel

Each row is one contract, and the Status column is the queue. The workflow picks up anything marked Ready to send and updates the status as the contract moves along. Your team gets one place to see where every contract stands.

Create a table in an Excel workbook stored in SharePoint or OneDrive, with these columns:

  • Status: Ready to send → Sent / Rejected → Signed
  • Client Name, Company, Email (the signer)
  • Amount, Start Date, plus Document ID and Signed At, which the workflow fills in

In the Microsoft Excel node, pick your workbook, worksheet, and table, then set Operation to Lookup, Lookup Column to Status, Lookup Value to Ready to send, and turn on Return All Matches.

👉
Not an Excel shop? Excel is just the queue. Any app with an n8n node that can read a record and update it works the same way: a CRM like Salesforce, HubSpot, Pipedrive, or Zoho CRM; a spreadsheet or database like Google Sheets, Airtable, Postgres, or n8n Data Table; or a project tool like monday.com or ClickUp. Swap the Excel steps for your app's node, map the same fields, and the approval, signature, and filing steps stay the same. With a CRM, you can also skip the 15-minute schedule and start the workflow the moment a deal moves to Closed Won. The other steps swap just as easily: approve in Microsoft Teams instead of Slack, or file signed PDFs to Google Drive, Dropbox, or OneDrive.

Step 2: Prepare the contract template

Start with the contract legal has already approved, as a regular Word .docx file. Replace the parts that change with merge variables like {clientName}, {amount}, and {startDate}.

Then add two anchors for the signature:

  • {client_sig} marks where the signer's signature goes.
  • {client_date} marks where the signing date is stamped.

Upload the file to TurboDocx and copy the template ID. Everything outside the variables stays exactly as legal wrote it.

Step 3: Generate the contract

Open the Generate Agreement Docx node, select your credential, and paste in the template ID. Then map each variable to its Excel column:

clientName    → {{ $json["Client Name"] }}amount → {{ $json["Amount"] }}startDate     → {{ $json["Start Date"] }}

Run the node on a test row. You'll get a finished contract back in a few seconds, formatted exactly like your template.

Step 4: Approve it in Slack

This step is where a person weighs in. The Slack node uses Send and Wait for Response to post the contract to your approvals channel with Approve & send and Reject buttons. The workflow waits until someone clicks one.

Edit the message so the approver has what they need to decide: the client, the value, and a link to the document. The If node sends approvals on to signature. Rejections get marked Rejected in Excel, and the team gets a heads-up.

Step 5: Send it for signature

This is the step that used to be tricky in n8n before. Once the contract is approved, the workflow passes the PDF to the Send Agreement for E-Signature node (TurboSign: Send Signature). Map the signer's name and email from the Excel row.

TurboSign places the signature and date fields at the {client_sig} and {client_date} anchors, so you never drag fields into place by hand. The signer gets an email and signs from any device. Meanwhile, the row flips to Sent.

Step 6: File the signed contract in SharePoint

Part B starts with the TurboDocx Trigger. Its webhook registers itself when you activate the workflow, so there's no URL to copy.

In the Microsoft SharePoint node, pick your site and your signed-contracts folder. When the client signs, the executed PDF is uploaded, the row is marked Signed, and Slack lets everyone know.

Step 7: Test it end to end

Before you point this at real clients, run one contract through yourself:

  1. Activate the workflow.
  2. Add a row to Excel with your own email as the signer and set it to Ready to send.
  3. Wait for the next scheduled run, or run the workflow manually.
  4. Click Approve & send in Slack.
  5. Sign the contract from your inbox.
  6. Check that the PDF is in SharePoint and the row says Signed.

If all six steps work, you're done. From here on, marking a row Ready to send and clicking Approve are the only manual steps left.

Troubleshooting

  • Signed contracts aren't being filed. Make sure the workflow is activated. The signature webhook only registers on activation.
  • Rows aren't being picked up. The status filter matches the text exactly, so check for typos and extra spaces in Ready to send.
  • No Slack message. Check that your Slack app has been added to the approvals channel.
  • Signature lands in the wrong spot. Check the anchor spelling in your template. It must be exactly {client_sig} and {client_date}.
  • Testing on self-hosted n8n fails with “TurboDocx webhooks require an HTTPS callback URL”. The signature trigger needs a public HTTPS address, which n8n Cloud provides out of the box. On a self-hosted instance, put n8n behind HTTPS (or a tunnel) and set WEBHOOK_URL to that address.

Why this works

Legal language can't drift. The clauses live in the template. The workflow only fills in the blanks.

Nothing goes out unapproved. Every contract waits for a click in Slack, and that approval is on record.

Nothing gets lost after signing. Every executed PDF lands in the same SharePoint folder, and the Excel row shows its status at a glance.

👉
 What it doesn't do (yet): As published, the template sends to one signer and doesn't handle redlines or back-and-forth negotiation. Contracts that need edits should go back through the template before they're marked Ready to send again.

Where to go from here

  • Swap the system of record. Trigger on a deal stage change in Salesforce or HubSpot instead of a schedule.
  • Let AI draft the variable sections. Add an OpenAI or Anthropic node before generation to write the business overview from your call notes. The clauses stay fixed.
  • Route by value. Send contracts over a set amount to a different approver or channel.
  • Signing quotes, not contracts? The same signature step works for sales quotes. See the CPQ quote template.

Wrap up

Contracts don't need more automation around the edges. They need the last step handled: getting the signature. With that in place, n8n can take a contract all the way from a spreadsheet row to a signed PDF in the right folder, with a person still making the call to send it.

Get this workflow

Download the template and send your first contract today with a free TurboDocx account.

Import the Template

We can't wait to see what you build.

Useful resources

  • TurboDocx node on n8n
  • TurboDocx e-signature for n8n
  • Contract e-signature template

item.title: Throttling vs. rate limiting: Backoff strategies for workflows
item.description: Throttling versus rate limiting changes how you respond to API limits. See how Retry-After, exponential backoff, and jitter make retries more reliable.
item.dc:creator: n8n team
item.content:encoded:
A burst of 429 (Too Many Requests) errors can bring an otherwise healthy workflow to a halt. Retrying is part of the solution, but timing matters: Retry too quickly and you’re likely to hit the same limit again.

Understanding throttling versus rate limiting helps you respond more intelligently, from pacing API calls upfront to backing off when the provider tells you to wait.

API throttling vs. rate limiting: Who enforces, who adapts

Rate limiting and throttling both control how much traffic reaches an API, but they don’t handle excess requests the same way. A rate limit sets a cap on how many requests a client can make within a given period. Once you cross that cap, the provider can reject additional requests, often with a 429 Too Many Requests response.

Throttling can instead slow or delay requests when traffic exceeds an allowed rate. Either way, the provider controls the limit. As the API consumer, you control how your workflow responds: pacing requests to avoid the limit where possible and backing off when you hit it.

What Is API throttling?

API throttling regulates request traffic by slowing its flow instead of just letting every request through at once. When demand gets too high, requests may be delayed or queued until capacity becomes available.

That doesn’t necessarily mean a request for your workflow fails just because the API is under pressure. But it can take longer to complete. Your workflow still needs to account for that delay, especially when later steps depend on the response.

Rate limiting vs. throttling: The practical difference

Imagine an API allows 100 requests per minute and your workflow sends request 101 before that minute is up. With rate limiting, that request may be rejected with a 429 error, leaving your workflow to decide when to try again. With throttling, the provider may hold request 101 in a queue and process it later instead.

That difference changes what your workflow sees (an error versus a delay) but not who’s in control. The API provider enforces the traffic policy. Your job is to adapt your request pattern so the workflow can keep moving without repeatedly overwhelming the service.

Scroll for more ➔
Rate limiting Throttling
What happens over the limit? Requests may be rejected Requests may be delayed or queued
What does your workflow see? An error (often error 429) A slower response
Who controls it? API provider API provider
What should your workflow do? Back off and retry Account for the added delay

How rate limits work

Rate limits sound simple — make too many requests, and the API tells you to stop. What counts as too many, though, depends on how the provider measures traffic. Some APIs count requests within a fixed period, while others allow short bursts as long as your overall request rate stays within bounds.

For your workflow, the underlying algorithm matters because it changes how you should pace requests. A steady stream of calls might work well against one API but run into limits with another. And when you do cross the line, you’ll often encounter Error 429 — your first clue that it’s time to slow down.

Fixed vs. sliding windows

A fixed-window rate limit divides time into set intervals. An API might allow 100 requests every minute, then reset the counter when the next minute begins. While this makes the rule easy to understand, it can allow sudden bursts around the boundary between two windows.

A sliding window avoids that hard reset by measuring requests over a continuously moving period. Instead of asking how many requests you’ve made since the timer began, it considers how many you’ve made over the previous 60 seconds. Waiting for the clock to roll over may not immediately restore your workflow’s full request allowance.

Token buckets vs. leaky buckets

Token bucket algorithms give you some room to burst. Think of your API allowance as a bucket that receives tokens at a steady rate. Each request spends a token, and unused tokens can accumulate up to the bucket’s capacity. If enough tokens have built up, your workflow can send several requests at once without exceeding the limit.

A leaky bucket takes the opposite approach. Requests enter a queue and leave at a controlled rate. Bursts get smoothed into a steadier flow instead of consuming accumulated capacity all at once.

Don’t assume every API rewards the same request pattern. Check the provider’s rate-limit documentation before deciding how aggressively to batch or pace calls.

What a 429 (Too Many Requests) error tells you

When an API rejects a request because you’ve exceeded its rate limit, HTTP status 429 (Too Many Requests) tells you what happened. The response may also include a Retry-After header indicating how long the client should wait before making another request.

If Retry-After is present, use it instead of guessing when to retry. If it’s not, your workflow needs its own strategy for spacing subsequent attempts. That’s where exponential backoff comes in: Instead of retrying at the same interval (or immediately), you progressively increase the delay between attempts.

Exponential backoff

When an API tells you to slow down, immediately retrying the same request can recreate the problem. Exponential backoff avoids that loop by increasing the wait after each failed attempt. Instead of retrying every second, for example, your workflow might wait one second, then two, four, eight, and so on.

Set a maximum delay and retry limit so temporary API issues don’t leave your workflow retrying indefinitely. If the API provides a Retry-After value, respect that guidance rather than relying solely on your own schedule.

There’s another wrinkle. Multiple workflows that fail together can also retry together. Adding jitter, or a small amount of randomness to each delay, spreads those attempts out and helps prevent another traffic spike.

Make sure the request is safe to repeat. Requests with side effects can accidentally perform an action twice, so check whether the API supports idempotency before automatically retrying them.

💡
Adding jitter is especially important when you work with AI agentic systems that use tools. Read our article on error handling for LLM tool calling, in which we explain when retries are possible and when it’s better to escalate the errors. 

Throttling and backoff patterns in n8n

You don’t need to build rate-limit handling from scratch. n8n is a source-available, AI-native automation platform that gives engineering several ways to handle rate limits with AI agents or agentic workflows. You can slow requests before they hit the API limit, retry after a failure, or route persistent errors elsewhere.

Handle API rate limits without building retry logic from scratch

Batch requests, add wait nodes, and route persistent 429s to error workflows — all on one canvas

Sign up for free

The right pattern depends on the API. You can batch and space requests to control traffic proactively, add waits between individual calls, or configure retries when an API responds with a 429. Concurrency controls can also cap parallel executions so multiple workflows don’t collectively overwhelm the same API. Pace requests first, then use retries and error handling as safeguards when limits still get in the way.

Pace requests with batching and wait nodes

For APIs with predictable limits, prevention is usually better than recovery. The HTTP Request node can process items in batches and pause between them using Items per Batch and Batch Interval. This lets you control how many requests go out at once and how long n8n waits before sending the next batch.

You can see the pattern in practice with this workflow for batching HTTP requests. When you need finer control, combine Loop Over Items with a Wait node to pace requests individually around the API’s limits.

Retry on fail with backoff

Pacing requests reduces the chance of hitting a limit, but it can’t prevent every 429. For those cases, Retry On Fail lets you automatically retry a failed node and configure the Wait Between Tries so you don’t immediately send the same request again.

For more complex cases, like increasing the delay between attempts, you can build more advanced retry logic into the workflow. This gives you control over when to try again and when to stop retrying altogether.

Catch persistent 429s with error workflows

Some requests will still fail after you’ve exhausted your retries. Instead of letting those failures disappear into the execution history, you can route them through a separate error workflow for logging, alerts, or other recovery steps.

With n8n, you can use the Error Trigger node to run a dedicated workflow when another workflow fails. That way, persistent 429 errors can trigger a defined recovery path instead of just ending the execution.

💡
Here's another guide on how to use the API rate limit to create more reliable workflows.

Take control of API rate limits with n8n

You can’t control the limits an API sets, but you can control how your workflow responds when it hits them. With n8n, that response becomes part of the workflow itself instead of custom retry code you have to build and maintain.

Take control of API rate limits with n8n

Pacing, retries, and error routing built directly into your workflow instead of custom code you have to maintain

Try n8n Cloud free

item.title: Why we're moving n8n's automation team beyond the service desk model
item.description: Romina da Costa, head of internal AI and automation at n8n, shares the four principles her team uses to help every team build and own its automations.
item.dc:creator: Romina da Costa
item.content:encoded:
In the first article of our n8n on n8n series, Romina da Costa, our head of internal AI and automation, explains where the service desk model hits its limit. She also shares the four principles her team now follows to help every team at n8n build and own its automations.

What does success look like for an automation team? Workflows shipped, tickets closed, backlog cleared? TLDR: none of that is actually what makes an automation team successful.

Every centralized automation team solves a real business problem: automating routine tasks, freeing up time, and taking on work that doesn't actually need human judgment. But solving that well is exactly what lets the rest of the organization lean on you to keep solving it, instead of building that capability into how the organization actually functions. You're not fixing the bottleneck. You're shifting it downstream.

This isn't a mistake unique to n8n, and I don't think it's really a mistake at all. Most organizations, especially at the enterprise level, are going to arrive at some version of this same realization. You stand up a centralized automation team. You clear the backlog. You free people from routine work. All of that genuinely works, for a while. What you're left holding afterward is a problem nobody budgeted for: who actually maintains everything you just built, and whether the team that solved the first problem can carry the second one indefinitely.

There's a bigger shift happening underneath this too. Building, workflows, agents, internal tools, is getting radically more accessible to people who aren't engineers. You'd think that makes a central automation team less necessary. I think it makes the job more important, just a different job. The scarce skill stops being "can you build this" and becomes "should this be built, how do you know it worked, which tool actually fits, and who owns it when it breaks." Easier building raises the stakes on judgment. It doesn't remove the need for it.

So here's what I actually think is the job of the Automation team, and why I've spent my first months here trying to change what success looks like for my team.

The automation team was working. But the model had reached its ceiling.

The Automation team was built to solve a real problem, well before I arrived. n8n's teams were drowning in manual work, and nobody was joined-up enough across the org to fix it systematically. So the company hired engineers to build workflows: connect tools, eliminate repetitive tasks, free people up for higher-value work. That was the right call for where the company was at the time, and the team did exactly what it was asked to do, and they did it remarkably well.

By the time I joined earlier this year to lead the function, I found a team whose own success and the company's growth had quietly exposed the limits of the model it was built on. We have somewhere north of 12,000 internal workflows and no team, however good, can build and maintain all of that. If "build more automations" were still the job description, I'd be running the very thing standing between the company and the outcome I was actually hired to accelerate.

That's the trap I'd flag to anyone stepping into a role like mine. It's not a failure of the previous team or the previous model. It's just where this function ends up if you let it run its natural course. That's fine, even expected. At some point, though, it becomes the job of whoever's leading AI and automation to step in and interrupt it, deliberately, before it goes too far. That's especially true if what you're actually trying to build is a highly automated, AI-first organization that's ready for how work is changing.

The reframe: From building automation to building an automation culture.

The question I've been sitting with isn't "how do we build more automations?" It's "how do I build a company where every team can think and act like automation engineers?" They sound similar, but they have completely different repercussions for how we approach the work, and what that work actually looks like.

Under the first question, success looks like throughput. Under the second, it looks like how many teams stop needing us at all. I've spent these early months trying to make that second answer the reality. That means figuring out what it actually takes to earn it: not just changing how my team works, but how we're perceived, and how other teams choose to interact with us in the first place. It sounds like a small shift on paper, but it changes almost everything about how we spend a given week.

In practice, that's turned into four principles.

1. Build the builders, not just the builds

The highest-leverage work my team does isn't the workflow they ship this week. It's the enablement that means a team doesn't need us the next time something similar comes up. That happens at a few different levels.

At the individual level, it looks like one of my engineers spending time this quarter not writing an automation for a stakeholder, but sitting with her while she debugged her own: reviewing why it failed, showing her what to change and why. The workflow got fixed either way. The difference is she won't need us next time.

At the team or department level, it looks like training sessions, reusable workflows other teams can start from instead of building blind, office hours where people bring a real problem and we build alongside them, and a network of technical champions: one person per department who understands their team's processes well enough to describe them clearly, and who owns the tools that team actually uses day to day. They don't need to be engineers. They need to be the person who can tell you why a process works the way it does, which turns out to be the harder skill to find.

Having one champion per department is a real starting point, not the end state. It's also useful in a way that goes beyond enablement: when a department doesn't have an obvious champion yet, that tells us something, both about where to focus next and about what we should actually be hiring for. The honest goal is bigger than one person per team. In an ideal world, most people would be able to act like a champion for their own function. We're not there yet. But we have to start somewhere, and one clear owner per department is a reasonable place to start.

At the company level, it looks like efforts like the AI fluency framework we are creating: shared standards and a common baseline of judgment about responsible AI use that don't depend on any one team to hold up.

From the outside, building for someone and building with them can look identical, especially if all you're counting is workflows shipped. Yet they're completely different jobs. Getting my team, and our stakeholders, to actually understand that difference has been most of my work these first few months.

2. Require a baseline before you build

This one came from a mistake I watched happen in real time. One of our AI agents generated a genuinely impressive result: six figures in the pipeline in a month. It felt like an obvious win, until I asked the question that actually mattered. Compared to what?

It wasn't that we had nothing to compare against. We had real numbers on what our human SDRs produced. The complication was that the comparison itself wasn't clean. The agent runs around the clock and never takes a break, and by that point our human SDRs were mostly handling the harder, escalated work the agent had already filtered out for them. Stacking the agent's raw pipeline number against the human SDRs’ wasn't actually comparing like with like, and figuring out what a fair comparison would even look like took real work.

I've since made it a hard requirement on my team. Before any new automation project starts, we ask the requesting team what today actually looks like: how often the work happens, how long it takes, how many people touch it, what it currently produces, and what would actually count as a meaningful improvement, even when the answers are only guesses. A guess is still more useful than nothing, and asking the question is often the first time anyone's thought about it at all.

3. Choose the tool for the problem, not the tool you're comfortable with

Once you actually know what you're trying to improve, the next question gets easier to answer: what's the right tool for this? We don't build for building's sake, and oftentimes, we push for a buy decision rather than building ourselves. This is the one that surprises people, given that we are n8n. As a general rule of thumb, if a proven, specific tool has existed on the market for a year or more, it's usually the better call over building internally, and the reasoning goes beyond which option works better today. Building it ourselves means taking on the maintenance burden and the security surface indefinitely, while a dedicated vendor team keeps shipping against their own roadmap while our V1 stops keeping up. A SaaS tool comes with an ongoing cost; building it ourselves just trades that for a different, less visible one: our own team's time, doing maintenance, upkeep and improvements, for as long as the thing exists. The real question isn't only which option works better right now. It's what we actually want to be responsible for maintaining and improving years from now.

The same discipline applies to agents versus workflows. Not every process needs an LLM in the loop. I've seen automation requests land on my team where the actual task was, functionally, "forward this email to James," dressed up as an agent, when a plain email filter would do the job with zero chance of getting it wrong. The discipline isn't avoiding agents. It's refusing to reach for one out of convenience or hype when a simpler, more predictable tool already solves the problem.

4. Make what we build resilient

Every workflow my team ships is a commitment, not a one-off favor. It needs an owner, documentation, error handling, and a plan for what happens when the person who built it moves onto something else, because eventually, they will. A clever automation nobody understands six months later becomes a liability.

This part is still aspirational. We don't have a single documentation standard the whole team follows yet, so one engineer's notes look nothing like another's, and that's a real cost the day someone has to pick up work that isn't theirs. We're working on a shared documentation template now, something every workflow gets measured against, and we're aiming to get it in place in the coming weeks. The harder part won't be writing the standard. It'll be actually enforcing it, making sure every workflow gets documented to the same bar instead of just the ones someone happened to make time for.

Transforming our model to transform the organisation

I don't want my team to be a service desk, a team that takes requests and delivers outputs on demand. I want us to solve the right problems in the right way. Sometimes that means building something. Sometimes it means teaching a team to build it themselves. Sometimes it means telling a stakeholder that what they've described isn't actually an automation problem yet.

That's the intent. We're not fully there. In practice, my team still functions like a service desk more often than I'd like, and the reason isn't really about process. It's that shifting culture is slow, and it's genuinely hard for people across a fast-moving company to find the time to learn how to build and own automations themselves. My team saying no more often doesn't fix that on its own. It takes real buy-in from leadership and from other functions: making AI fluency part of how people are evaluated, setting goals that get specific about how each function uses AI and automation, and building a culture where every team expects to own some of this, not just request it from us. That part isn't mine to solve alone, but it’s one I am working crossfunctionally to influence.

The switch in mandate

None of this makes a central automation team pointless once building gets easier for everyone. It changes when and why we get involved. My team should still own the problems that are complex, risky, or shared across the whole company, the kind of thing you don't want a dozen departments solving a dozen different ways. Everywhere else, our job is building the foundations, standards, and judgment that let other teams build responsibly without our direct involvement.

Giving people the ability to build is becoming the easy part. Every tool, including ours, is making that true faster than most of us expected. The harder part, the part our jobs are evolving into, is building an organization that knows what's worth building, how to build it well, and how to own it once it's built.

Romina da Costa leads Internal AI & Automation at n8n. Since joining, she has been restructuring the function from a workflow-building team into an enablement engine.

item.title: Introducing n8n 3.0
item.description: n8n 3.0 beta is out, focused on reliability, stability and security. Here’s what’s changing and how to get ready.
item.dc:creator: Ophir Prusak
item.content:encoded:
Today we're releasing n8n version 3.0.0 BETA

n8n 3.0 focuses on internal changes that improve reliability, stability and security, and lays the groundwork for the improvements we're building next. It clears out legacy features, tightens security defaults and reworks parts of how n8n runs under the hood.

The short version: the beta is available today and the stable release follows in early December. Because 3.0 includes breaking changes, some workflows and settings may need updates before you upgrade. The Migration Report in your instance tells you exactly which ones.

It’s worth taking a look now, even if you’re not planning to upgrade right away.

Why change the version number?

n8n follows semantic versioning. That means we don't ship breaking changes (updates that might require you to change your workflows or configuration) without bumping the major version number.

Over the past year we collected a list of breaking changes we wanted to make: legacy code paths to remove, defaults to make safer, a few features to retire. Each of them had to wait for a major version, so 3.0 brings them together in one release.

If you're wondering where the new features went, they didn't wait. We ship features continuously instead of saving them for a major version. Since 2.0 came out in December 2025, we've shipped over 45 releases, roughly one a week, and many of them included major new features. The full list is on our changelog.

That's why 3.0 can focus purely on the foundation, and everything new after the stable release ships on 3.x.

What's in version 3.0

The 3.0 breaking changes docs have a detailed list with what to do for each change. Here are the main themes, with a few examples.

Reliability and stability

  • Queue mode. Manual executions now always run on workers, so the main instance isn't doing that work.
  • Binary data. The in-memory binary data mode is removed. Instances use the filesystem, or S3 and other external storage, which is more predictable under load.
  • Guardrails against runaway work. The default Code node timeout (task runner) drops from 5 minutes to 1 minute, and it's configurable. Decompression limits are lower, to protect instances from oversized archives ("zip bombs").
  • Scheduling. The old Cron and Interval nodes are replaced by the Schedule Trigger, which runs on n8n's more durable scheduler.

Security

We made several defaults safer:

  • Encryption key rotation is always on.
  • Slack credentials require a signing secret, so nobody can send forged requests pretending to be Slack.
  • A larger default SSRF (server-side request forgery) block list when SSRF protection is enabled.
  • Unverified community packages are off by default.

Self-hosting

Self-hosted n8n now runs on Docker. Installing with npm or npx n8n is no longer supported, partly because new security features depend on a container setup. If you liked npx n8n for how quick it was, there's a one-line setup script that gets you to the same place. Kubernetes and Helm deployments aren't affected.

Cleanup

We removed legacy nodes: Function, Function Item, Item Lists, Cron, Interval, the legacy OpenAI node, older AI Agent modes, older versions of the Edit Image node, nodes for services that no longer exist, and others. Most have a direct replacement (Function becomes the Code node; Item Lists becomes Split Out, Aggregate, Sort, Limit, Remove Duplicates or Summarize), and many migrate automatically.

A few features are retired too. Chat Hub is off by default (you can turn it back on for 3.x; the n8n AI assistant and agents are replacing it), Import from URL is gone from the editor, and the Ask AI tab is gone from the Code node.

Check if you're ready: the Migration Report

This is the part I'd read if I read nothing else.

Every instance on version 2.39 or later has a Migration Report under Settings > Migration Report.

The latest 2.x version has the newest version of the report and we'll continue to improve the experience as we get more feedback, so update first.

Here's what it does:

  • Lists the workflows and instance-level settings affected by 3.0.
  • Fixes many issues automatically. Each fix is saved as a new workflow version for you to review and publish, and your published workflows keep running on v2 while you work.
  • Suggests an owner for each workflow (whoever edited it last), lets admins reassign, and emails owners what to fix.
  • Filters out workflows that aren't published or haven't run in a long time, so you can mark those "won't fix" and move on.
  • Exports a CSV summary.

Admins see every workflow; other users see the workflows they have access to. Unlike last year, you don't need to be an admin to see it.

The path we recommend:

  1. Update to the latest 2.x and open the Migration Report.
  2. Fix, or mark "won't fix", everything it flags.
  3. Take a full backup.
  4. Upgrade a test or staging instance first, then production.

Check out the detailed v3 Migration Tool Docs

Try the beta today

No sign-up needed.

  • Self-hosted: install it like any other beta release.
  • n8n Cloud: pick 3.0.0 Beta (early access) when changing your n8n version.

One thing to know before you click: moving to 3.x is one way. There's no going back to 2.x. Try it on a test instance first, and take a full backup.

A year since 2.0

It's only been a year, but the numbers are worth a look.

  • GitHub stars: from about 160,000 at the 2.0 release to over 208,000 today.
  • Community forum members: from 115,192 to over 183,000.

Behind those numbers are the people who file issues, build nodes, answer questions in the forum, write tutorials, and tell us when something broke. Thank you for all of it.

FAQ: What you need to know

When is this happening?
Beta (3.0.0) today, October 27. Stable (3.x) in early December. Follow the release notes for updates.

What are the breaking changes?
Here are all of them, with what to do for each, are in the 3.0 breaking changes docs.

How do I know if I'm affected?
Open the Migration Report under Settings > Migration Report (version 2.39 or later).

Does the Community edition get all 3.0 updates?
Yes. Everything in 3.0 applies to self-hosted Community, Cloud, and Enterprise/Business.

What happens to 2.x?
After the stable release, 2.x gets security and critical bug fixes for 12 months. New features ship on 3.x only.

I'm still on 1.x. What do I do?
Upgrade to 2.x first; there's no direct path from 1.x to 3.x. Support for 1.x ends December 31, 2026.

Can I roll back?
No. Take a full backup before upgrading; going back means restoring it.

Is there downtime?
A short restart, like any upgrade.

Do my credentials and execution history carry over?
Yes.

What if I have questions?
Reply to the announcement thread in the community forum and we'll help you out.

Thanks from Ophir and all of the n8n team!

item.title: AI agent memory: How LLM agents manage state in production
item.description: Learn how AI agent memory works, explore short-term and long-term memory architectures, and discover how to combine n8n and Cognee to build AI workflows that retain context, share knowledge, and learn across sessions.
item.dc:creator: n8n team
item.content:encoded:
💡
This is a guest post written by Veljko Kovac, Head of FDE at Cognee, an open-source agent memory platform.

Every LLM call starts from zero

An LLM has no memory of its own. Each request is independent: the model reads the prompt, returns a response, and keeps nothing. Send a second request and, as far as the model knows, the first never happened.

That is fine for a one-shot question. It breaks down the moment you build something that works over time: a support agent handling a follow-up, a sales assistant prepping for a renewal call, or a workflow that runs every hour and should know what it did last time. These systems need state, and the model can't hold it for them.

So when people ask how LLM memory works, the honest answer is that the memory lives outside the model. The agent stores what it learns somewhere else, retrieves the relevant parts before each call, and feeds them back into the prompt. That external layer is what we call AI agent memory, and how you design it decides whether your agent remembers the right things or drowns in the wrong ones.

This post explains how that layer works, the main ways to build it, and how to use it in n8n, both as a shared "company brain" your workflows can query and as memory inside a single agentic workflow.

Short-term and long-term memory

Agent memory usually works on two timescales, and they are often built as two separate components.

Short-term memory keeps track of what's happening right now: recent messages, intermediate reasoning, tool outputs, the state of the task. It lives close to the agent, often inside the harness itself. When the context window fills up, a common trick is to summarize the history so far and feed the summary back in. That works until it doesn't: summaries lose detail, and some outputs shouldn't be compressed at all, for example intermediate drafts or the results of expensive computations.

Long-term memory survives across sessions. It holds user preferences, outcomes of past tasks, lessons about what worked, and increasingly, company knowledge the agent didn't generate itself: docs, tickets, CRM records. This almost always needs a dedicated external layer from day one, because something has to decide what gets kept, how it's organized, and what comes back for each request.

Either way, the delivery mechanism doesn't change. The model still receives one prompt. Memory just changes how that prompt is assembled: the new user message, plus the running session, plus whatever long-term memories are relevant right now.

LLM memory, context, RAG, agent memory: what's the difference?

These four terms get used interchangeably, but they describe different places where knowledge can live. A real system often uses all of them.

Approach

Where knowledge lives

Who updates it

Good for

LLM memory (model weights)

Inside the model

Training or fine-tuning

Context engineering

RAG

Grounding answers in existing knowledge

Agent memory

An external memory layer that keeps evolving

People, data pipelines, and the agent itself

Continuity across tasks, sessions and sources

LLM memory in the strict sense is what the model absorbed during training. It's compressed patterns, not a lookup table, which is why a model can confidently repeat something outdated. Fine-tuning can add domain knowledge, but it's slow, expensive, hard to inspect, and it can't capture anything from a live session.

Context engineering is choosing what goes into the context window for this particular call. Bigger windows help, but they don't solve memory: the context vanishes when the session ends, long prompts cost more, and models don't attend equally to everything in a very long input.

RAG retrieves from an existing knowledge source (docs, a database, an API) and adds the results to the prompt. The key limitation is direction: RAG reads, but it doesn't write back. It won't remember what the user asked last week or which fix already failed.

Agent memory starts where the agent writes back. It captures new facts, preferences and outcomes as it works, and retrieves them later. Picture a sales assistant that pulls this quarter's numbers via RAG, but also remembers from earlier conversations that this user wants EU figures in euros, broken down by country. 

How agent memory actually works

At a high level, any memory system needs three pieces: a data store where memories are persisted, write logic that decides what gets stored and how,  and a retrieval interface that lets the agent find the relevant memories. The store you choose has a big influence on the other two: which write logic makes sense, and what retrieval can do. So here are the main architectures, by store type.

Vector databases. Memories are turned into embeddings and found by semantic similarity. Easy to set up and well supported, but similarity isn't everything. "Q3 sales" and "Q4 sales" sit almost on top of each other in vector space, there's no notion of which fact is current, and an entry that's relevant but phrased differently can be missed entirely.

Plain files. The agent keeps a MEMORY.md (or similar) that it reads and edits. Coding agents popularized this. It's transparent and version-controlled, but retrieval is limited to loading everything or grep-ping, and sharing a file between many agents gets messy fast.

Knowledge graphs. Facts become entities and relationships: the sales report covers EU deals, EU deals are booked in euros, the figures come from the billing export. Retrieval finds an entry point, then follows the edges, so the agent gets facts that are logically related to the question, not only ones that sound similar. The trade-off is more work at ingestion time.

Hybrid systems. In practice, no single store covers everything. Exact IDs want a structured index, relationships want a graph, fuzzy matching wants vectors, and "what did the customer prefer last March?" needs timestamps. Production memory layers combine stores and put logic on top that decides what goes where. This is also why a memory layer is more than a database: the stores are just where the data lives, and the memory layer sits on top of them. It decides what gets stored and in what form, and exposes the operations agents use to write, retrieve, update and forget.

Architecture

Retrieval

Strength

Watch out for

Vector database

Semantic similarity

Simple, scalable, mature tooling

No entities, weak on exact IDs, no recency

Load all or search text

Transparent, versioned, no infra

Doesn't scale or share well

Hybrid
